results.prompt: Explain the singleton dependency type for Slurm jobs
results.agent_response:
Brief summary
- The singleton dependency ensures at most one job with the same user + job name is allowed to be active at a time.  
- When you submit a job with --dependency=singleton (or #SBATCH --dependency=singleton), Slurm implicitly delays that job until any earlier job(s) with the same user and the same job name have finished. Once those earlier job(s) exit (in any final state), the singleton job becomes eligible to start.

Why and when to use it
- Use singleton when you want serialized execution of jobs that share the same job name (for example periodic jobs, or multiple submissions of the same workflow) and you don’t want two of them running concurrently.
- It is a lightweight alternative to manually creating after: dependencies between specific job IDs.

Behavior notes / gotchas
- The “same job” is matched by job name and submitting user. Jobs with a different name or user are not considered.
- The dependency is satisfied when the earlier job terminates in any final state (i.e., success or failure). It does not require a successful exit.
- It only affects jobs that include the singleton dependency; other jobs without that dependency are unaffected and can run concurrently.
- If you submit many singleton jobs in sequence, they will effectively run one at a time in the order Slurm resolves them.
- Don’t rely on singleton for complex ordering across different job names or users—use explicit job-ID dependencies (after, afterok, afterany, etc.) when you need precise control.

How to set it
- sbatch --dependency=singleton myscript.sh
- or in a batch script: #SBATCH --dependency=singleton

If you want, I can show the exact manpage wording or examples from the Slurm docs.

results.prompt: Explain the singleton dependency type for Slurm jobs
results.agent_response:
What it is
- The singleton dependency tells Slurm “only start this job once all previously launched jobs with the same job name and the same user have finished (ended).”
- In short: it serializes jobs by (user, job-name) so at most one job with that name from that user is running at a time.

How to use it
- Specify it with sbatch --dependency=singleton (the job name comes from --job-name or the script filename).
- Example:
  sbatch --dependency=singleton --job-name=mytask myscript.sh

Behavior and semantics
- “Previously launched” means jobs submitted earlier than this job. The dependent job will not become eligible until those earlier jobs with the same name and user have ended (completed, failed, cancelled, timed out — any terminal state).
- It does not require you to list job IDs; the dependency is resolved by matching job name and user.
- Ordering is by submission: later singleton jobs wait for earlier ones to terminate before running.
- It does not enforce exclusivity across different users or different job names.

When to use it
- Serializing a series of jobs that must not run concurrently (e.g., to avoid simultaneous writes to the same output file).
- Collating results or sending one notification after a swarm of jobs with the same name finishes.

Limitations / notes
- If you need a dependency tied to a specific job’s success/failure, use afterok/afternotok/afterany with job IDs instead.
- Singleton works at the (user, job-name) granularity only; it cannot enforce a cluster-wide single instance across different users.

In your Slurm build directory, navigate to contribs/nss_slurm/
and run:

make && make install

to the directory which includes your other NSS plugins to enable it.

recommended, and for RHEL-based distributions
/usr/lib64 is recommended. If in doubt,
a command such as

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Snippet:
## Consumable Resource Examples [#example3](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
The following two examples illustrate the primary difference between
CR_CPU and CR_Core when consumable resource selection is enabled
( select/cons_tres ).
When CR_CPU (or CR_CPU_Memory ) is configured then the selector
treats the CPUs as simple, interchangeable computing resources
unless task affinity is enabled. However when task affinity is enabled
with CR_CPU or CR_Core (or CR_Core_Memory ) is enabled, the
selector treats the CPUs as individual resources that are specifically
allocated to jobs.
This subtle difference is highlighted when timeslicing is enabled.

If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.

complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

## Versioning [#versioning](https://slurm.schedmd.com/plugins.html)
Slurm plugins must provide a plugin_version symbol exactly matching that
of the process they are loaded into. This is to avoid any potential issues if,
e.g., an underlying struct definition is changed by a maintenance release.
It is expected that the plugins are automatically build, packaged, and
distributed alongside the libslurm library, Slurm commands, and daemons.
The only exception to this is the SPANK plugin interface which only requires
the Slurm release to match, while the maintenance release (micro version) may be
changed. This is to reflect the additional ABI stability commitment that is
maintained exclusively for that plugin interface.

document.querySelector('title').textContent = ' Building pipelines using slurm dependencies'; 
 
Building pipelines using slurm dependencies 
 
 
 
 Quick Links 
 Introduction 
 Bash 
 Perl 
 Python 
 

 
 
 Differences between stock sbatch and sbatch on biowulf 

 
 Before discussing job dependencies we need to point out that
 sbatch on biowulf, and therefore in the examples below, is a
 wrapper script that returns just the jobid. That is different
 from stock sbatch which returns Submitted batch job 123456 .
 You can think of the wrapper doing something equivalent to 

 
#! /bin/bash

sbr="$(/path/to/real/sbatch "$@")"

if [[ "$sbr" =~ Submitted\ batch\ job\ ([0-9]+) ]]; then
 echo "${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
 exit 0
else
 echo "sbatch failed"
 exit 1
fi
 
 

 

 
 
 Introduction 

 
Job dependencies are used to defer the start of a job until the specified
dependencies have been satisfied. They are specified with the 
 --dependency option to sbatch or swarm 
in the format
 

 
sbatch --dependency=<type:job_id[:job_id][,type:job_id[:job_id]]> ...
 

 Dependency types: 
 
 after :jobid[:jobid...] 
 job can begin after the specified jobs have started 
 
 afterany :jobid[:jobid...] 
 job can begin after the specified jobs have terminated 
 
 afternotok :jobid[:jobid...] 
 job can begin after the specified jobs have failed 
 
 afterok :jobid[:jobid...] 
 job can begin after the specified jobs have run to completion
 with an exit code of zero (see the 
 user guide for
 caveats). 
 
 singleton 
 jobs can begin execution after all previously launched jobs 
 with the same name and user have ended. This is useful to collate
 results of a swarm or to send a notification at the end of a swarm. 
 
 

 See also the Job Dependencies 
section of the User Guide . 

 To set up pipelines using job dependencies the most useful types are 
afterany, afterok and singleton. The simplest way is to use the afterok
dependency for single consecutive jobs. For example:
 
 
b2$ sbatch job1.sh 
11254323
b2$ sbatch --dependency=afterok:11254323 job2.sh 
 

 Now when job1 ends with an exit code of zero, job2 will become eligible for
scheduling. However, if job1 fails (ends with a non-zero exit code), job2 will
not be scheduled and will be canceled automatically by the scheduler.
 
 As an alternative, the afterany dependency can be used and checking for
successful execution of the prerequisites can be done in the jobscript itself.
 
 The sections below give more complicated examples of using job dependencies
for pipelines in bash, perl, and python. 

 
 
 Bash 

 The following bash script is a stylized example of some useful patterns
for using job dependencies: 

 
#! /bin/bash

# first job - no dependencies
jid1=$(sbatch --mem=12g --cpus-per-task=4 job1.sh)

# multiple jobs can depend on a single job
jid2=$(sbatch --dependency=afterany:$jid1 --mem=20g job2.sh)
jid3=$(sbatch --dependency=afterany:$jid1 --mem=20g job3.sh)

# a single job can depend on multiple jobs
jid4=$(sbatch --dependency=afterany:$jid2:$jid3 job4.sh)

# swarm can use dependencies
jid5=$(swarm --dependency=afterany:$jid4 -t 4 -g 4 -f job5.sh)

# a single job can depend on an array job
# it will start executing when all arrayjobs have finished
jid6=$(sbatch --dependency=afterany:$jid5 job6.sh)

# a single job can depend on all jobs by the same user with the same name
jid7=$(sbatch --dependency=afterany:$jid6 --job-name=dtest job7.sh)
jid8=$(sbatch --dependency=afterany:$jid6 --job-name=dtest job8.sh)
sbatch --dependency=singleton --job-name=dtest job9.sh

# show dependencies in squeue output:
squeue -u $USER -o "%.8A %.4C %.10m %.20E"

processes, 4 MPI processes ... 128 MPI processes. The Slurm batch script
'jobscript' uses the environment variable $SLURM_NTASKS to specify t

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.

## Coordinator[#coord](https://slurm.schedmd.com/user_permissions.html)
A special privileged user, usually an account manager, that can add
users or sub-accounts to the account they are coordinator over.
This should be a trusted person since they can change limits on account and
user associations, as well as cancel, requeue or reassign accounts of jobs
inside their realm. Note that a coordinator may not increase job limits above
the parent ones.
Set using a table in Slurm's database defining users and accounts for
which they can serve as coordinators.

[sacctmgr](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html) man page.

job_container.conf is an ASCII file which defines parameters used by
Slurm's namespace/tmpfs plugin. Based on these parameters, the plugin will
create the appropriate job-specifc namespace(s).
The namespace/tmpfs plugin creates a filesystem namespace and will construct a
private (or optionally shared) filesystem namespace and mount a list of
directories (defaults to /tmp and /dev/shm) inside it, giving the job a private
view of these directories. These paths are mounted inside the location specified
by 'BasePath' in the job_container.conf file.
When the job completes, the namespace is unmounted and all files therein are
automatically removed.

## Plugins[#Plugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/programmer_guide.html)
To make the use of different infrastructures possible, Slurm uses a general
purpose plugin mechanism. A Slurm plugin is a dynamically linked code object that
is loaded explicitly at run time by the Slurm libraries. It provides a customized
implementation of a well-defined API connected to tasks such as authentication,
interconnect fabric, task scheduling, etc. A set of functions is defined for use
by all of the different infrastructures of a particular variety. When a Slurm
daemon is initiated, it reads the configuration file to determine which of the
available plugins should be used. A [plugin developer's guide](https://slurm.schedmd.com/plugins.html) is available with general information about plugins.

"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login

The HDF5 Profile Plugin requires a common shared file system on all
the compute nodes. While a job is running, the plugin writes a
file into this file system for each step of the job on each node. When

allow users to define their own defaults for jobs submitted from the machine(s)

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

Snippet:
## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Requesting container jobs or steps [#request](https://slurm.schedmd.com/containers.html)
salloc , srun and sbatch (in Slurm 21.08+) have the
'--container' argument, which can be used to request container runtime

## Heterogeneous Steps [#het_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Slurm version 20.11 introduces the ability to request heterogeneous job
steps from within a non-homogeneous job allocation. This allows you the
flexibility to have different layouts for job steps without requiring the
use of heterogeneous jobs, where having separate jobs for the components
may be undesirable.
Some limitations for heterogeneous steps are that the steps must be able
to run on unique nodes. You also cannot request heterogeneous steps from within
a heterogeneous job.

job_container.conf is an ASCII file which defines parameters used by
Slurm's namespace/tmpfs plugin. Based on these parameters, the plugin will
create the appropriate job-specifc namespace(s).
The namespace/tmpfs plugin creates a filesystem namespace and will construct a

The first step of the process is to create a job allocation, which is

A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

## Versioning [#versioning](https://slurm.schedmd.com/plugins.html)
Slurm plugins must provide a plugin_version symbol exactly matching that
of the process they are loaded into. This is to avoid any potential issues if,
e.g., an underlying struct definition is changed by a maintenance release.
It is expected that the plugins are automatically build, packaged, and
distributed alongside the libslurm library, Slurm commands, and daemons.
The only exception to this is the SPANK plugin interface which only requires
the Slurm release to match, while the maintenance release (micro version) may be
changed. This is to reflect the additional ABI stability commitment that is
maintained exclusively for that plugin interface.

# Slurm Workload Manager
Slurm is an open-source workload manager designed for Linux clusters of
all sizes.
It provides three key functions.
First it allocates exclusive and/or non-exclusive access to resources
(computer nodes) to users for some duration of time so they can perform work.
Second, it provides a framework for starting, executing, and monitoring work
(typically a parallel job) on a set of allocated nodes.
Finally, it arbitrates contention for resources by managing a queue of
pending work.
Slurm's design is very modular with dozens of optional plugins.
In its simplest configuration, it can be installed and configured in a
couple of minutes (see [Caos NSA and Perceus: All-in-one Cluster Software Stack](http://www.linux-mag.com/id/7239/1/)
by Jeffrey B. Layton).
More complex configurations can satisfy the job scheduling needs of
world-class computer centers and rely upon a

The namespace/linux plugin (added 25.11) uses the configuration file
[namespace.yaml](https://slurm.schedmd.com/namespace.yaml.html). This plugin can be configured

namespace. Namespaces can be configured for all nodes or for a subset of nodes.

following in your namespace.yaml:

defaults: auto_base_path: true base_path: "/var/nvme/storage"

If any parameters in namespace.yaml are changed while slurm is running, then
slurmd on the respective nodes will need to be
restarted for changes to take effect (scontrol reconfigure is not sufficient).

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

## Job Submission [#jobsubmission](https://slurm.schedmd.com/federation.html)
When a federated cluster receives a job submission, it will submit copies of the
job ( sibling jobs ) to each eligible cluster. Each cluster will then
independently attempt to schedule the job.
Jobs can be directed to specific clusters in the federation using the
-M,--clusters=<cluster_list> and the new
--cluster-constraint=[!]<constraint_list> options.
Using the -M,--clusters=<cluster_list> the submission command
(sbatch, salloc, srun) will pick one cluster from the list of clusters to submit
the job to and will also pass along the list of clusters with the job. The
clusters in the list will be the only viable clusters that siblings jobs can be
submitted to. For example the submission:
```text
cluster1$ sbatch -Mcluster2,cluster3 script.sh
```
will submit the job to either cluster2 or cluster3 and will only submit sibling
jobs to cluster2 and cluster3 even if...

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Slurm environment variables will be set independently for each component of

## Heterogeneous Steps [#het_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Slurm version 20.11 introduces the ability to request heterogeneous job
steps from within a non-homogeneous job allocation. This allows you the
flexibility to have different layouts for job steps without requiring the
use of heterogeneous jobs, where having separate jobs for the components
may be undesirable.
Some limitations for heterogeneous steps are that the steps must be able
to run on unique nodes. You also cannot request heterogeneous steps from within
a heterogeneous job.
An example scenario would be if you have a task that needs to use 1 GPU
per processor while another task needs all the available GPUs on a node with
only one processor. This can be accomplished like this:
```text
$ salloc -N2 --exclusive --gpus=10 salloc: Granted job allocation 61034 $ srun -N1 -n4 --gpus=4 printenv SLURMD_NODENAME : -N1 -n1 --gpus=6 printenv SLURMD_NODENAME...

## Job Accounting Records [#job_record](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)
When Slurm is configured to use SlurmDBD to store job records (i.e.
AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage=slurmdbd ), there are multiple
records that get stored for each job. There is a record for the job as a
whole as well as entries for the following types of job steps:
- extern step — A step created for each job as long as you have PrologFlags=contain in your slurm.conf. Each node in the job will have a slurmstepd process created for the extern step. pam_slurm_adopt uses this step to contain external connections.
- batch step — A step created for jobs that were submitted with sbatch. The batch host, or the primary node for the job, will run an instance of slurmstepd for the batch step, which is used to run the script provided to sbatch.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Slurm environment variables will be set independently for each component of
the job by appending "_HET_GROUP_" and a sequence number to the usual name.

components in the job. Note that if using srun with a single specific

## Job Accounting Records [#job_record](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)
When Slurm is configured to use SlurmDBD to store job records (i.e.
AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage=slurmdbd ), there are multiple
records that get stored for each job. There is a record for the job as a
whole as well as entries for the following types of job steps:
- extern step — A step created for each job as long as you have PrologFlags=contain in your slurm.conf. Each node in the job will have a slurmstepd process created for the extern step. pam_slurm_adopt uses this step to contain external connections.
- batch step — A step created for jobs that were submitted with sbatch. The batch host, or the primary node for the job, will run an instance of slurmstepd for the batch step, which is used to run the script provided to sbatch.

## Launching Applications (Job Steps) [#job_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The srun command is used to launch applications.
By default, the application is launched only on the first component of a
heterogeneous job, but options are available to support different behaviors.
srun's "--het-group" option defines which hetjob component(s) are to have
applications launched for them. The --het-group option takes an expression
defining which component(s) are to launch an application for an individual
execution of the srun command. The expression can contain one or more component
index values in a comma separated list. Ranges of index values can be specified
in a hyphen separated list. By default, an application is launched only on
component number zero. Some examples follow:
- --het-group=2

## Heterogeneous Steps [#het_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
Slurm version 20.11 introduces the ability to request heterogeneous job
steps from within a non-homogeneous job allocation. This allows you the
flexibility to have different layouts for job steps without requiring the
use of heterogeneous jobs, where having separate jobs for the components
may be undesirable.
Some limitations for heterogeneous steps are that the steps must be able
to run on unique nodes. You also cannot request heterogeneous steps from within
a heterogeneous job.
An example scenario would be if you have a task that needs to use 1 GPU
per processor while another task needs all the available GPUs on a node with
only one processor. This can be accomplished like this:
```text
$ salloc -N2 --exclusive --gpus=10 salloc: Granted job allocation 61034 $ srun -N1 -n4 --gpus=4 printenv SLURMD_NODENAME : -N1 -n1 --gpus=6 printenv SLURMD_NODENAME...

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.
```text
#!/bin/bash #SBATCH --nodes=1 --constraint=haswell #BB create_persistent name=alpha capacity=10 access=striped type=scratch #DW persistentdw name=alpha #SBATCH hetjob #SBATCH --nodes=16 --constraint=knl #DW persistentdw name=alpha ...

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_container.conf.html)
job_container.conf is an ASCII file which defines parameters used by
Slurm's namespace/tmpfs plugin. Based on these parameters, the plugin will
create the appropriate job-specifc namespace(s).
The namespace/tmpfs plugin creates a filesystem namespace and will construct a
private (or optionally shared) filesystem namespace and mount a list of
directories (defaults to /tmp and /dev/shm) inside it, giving the job a private
view of these directories. These paths are mounted inside the location specified
by 'BasePath' in the job_container.conf file.
When the job completes, the namespace is unmounted and all files therein are
automatically removed.
To make use of this plugin, 'PrologFlags=Contain' must also be present in
your slurm.conf file, as shown:
```text
NamespaceType=namespace/tmpfs PrologFlags=Contain

slurm.conf is an ASCII file which describes general Slurm
configuration information, the nodes to be managed, information about
how those nodes are grouped into partitions, and various scheduling
parameters associated with those partitions. This file should be
consistent across all nodes in the cluster.
The file location can be modified at execution time by setting the SLURM_CONF
environment variable. The Slurm daemons also allow you to override
both the built-in and environment-provided location using the "-f"
option on the command line.
The contents of the file are case insensitive except for the names of nodes
and partitions. Any text following a "#" in the configuration file is treated
as a comment through the end of that line.

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.

config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by
either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV

Slurm version 20.11 introduces the ability to request heterogeneous job
steps from within a non-homogeneous job allocation. This allows you the
flexibility to have different layouts for job steps without requiring the

results.prompt: Explain the singleton dependency type for Slurm jobs
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- dependency=singleton serializes jobs so only one job from the same “singleton group” can be active at a time. Use it by passing --dependency=singleton to sbatch or srun for batch submissions.

What it does (semantics)
- When you submit a job with --dependency=singleton, Slurm will not start that job while another job in the same singleton group is still active (pending or running). The newly submitted job is held in the queue and becomes eligible only after the earlier job has finished (regardless of that job’s exit code).
- In practice the singleton group is determined by the submitting user and the job name (the job-name given with --job-name / -J). In other words, jobs with the same user and same job name are serialized by singleton.

How it differs from other dependencies
- singleton waits for completion of the earlier job(s) regardless of success or failure. Contrast that with afterok (which requires the predecessor to exit successfully) or afterany (which requires completion but is expressed with explicit job IDs).
- singleton is about preventing concurrent runs of “the same” job, not about sequencing specific job IDs.

Typical uses
- Prevent overlapping runs of a periodic task or workflow (for example, ensure a nightly data-processing job never runs concurrently with a previous run).
- Ensure only one instance of a named worker/ingest job is active per user.

Usage example
- sbatch --job-name=myjob --dependency=singleton myjob.sh

Notes and caveats
- singleton does not stop multiple submissions; it only delays start time so jobs run one at a time.
- It is enforced by the scheduler; it does not change job exit behavior or automatically cancel jobs.
- If you need sequencing that depends on success/failure, use afterok/afternotok/afterany instead.

If you want, I can show an example workflow or compare singleton behavior with a real pending job using squeue.

results.prompt: What does sbatch --parsable return and why is it useful?
results.agent_response:
What it returns
- sbatch --parsable prints a machine-readable job identifier on stdout instead of the human message ("Submitted batch job NNN"). On success sbatch still exits with status 0.

Notes on the identifier
- For a regular submission it is the Slurm job ID. For array submissions it returns the array-style identifier (the array master/job info) in a compact, script-friendly form.

Why it's useful
- Makes automation reliable: scripts can capture the exact job ID without brittle text parsing.
- Lets you programmatically chain actions (dependencies, squeue/sacct queries, scancel, etc.) by using the captured ID directly.
- Avoids locale or wording differences that break grep/awk on the normal human-oriented output.

Example (shell)
- JOBID=$(sbatch --parsable myscript.sh)
- squeue -j "$JOBID"   # or sbatch --dependency=afterok:$JOBID

These uses let CI, workflow engines, and shell scripts track and control jobs robustly.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text

```text

```

results.prompt: What does sbatch --parsable return and why is it useful?
results.agent_response:
sbatch --parsable makes sbatch print a machine-readable job identifier instead of the human text "Submitted batch job <id>". Concretely:

- For a normal batch submission it prints the job ID only (no extra words).

Why it's useful
- Easy to capture in scripts: jid=$(sbatch --parsable my.job) reliably returns the job id with no text to strip.
- Feed directly to other Slurm commands: use that id for dependencies (--dependency), cancellations (scancel), queries (squeue/scontrol), or bookkeeping.
- Avoids fragile text parsing of sbatch's human-readable output when automating job workflows.

## File Names[#file_names](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Two additional options are available to specify a job's stdin, stdout, and
stderr file names:
%A will be replaced by the value of SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID (as defined above)
and
%a will be replaced by the value of SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (as defined above).
The default output file format for a job array is "slurm-%A_%a.out".
An example of explicit use of the formatting is:
sbatch -o slurm-%A_%a.out --array=1-3 -N1 tmp
which would generate output files names of this sort
"slurm-36_1.out", "slurm-36_2.out" and "slurm-36_3.out".
If these file name options are used without being part of a job array then
"%A" will be replaced by the current job ID and "%a" will be replaced by
4,294,967,294 (equivalent to 0xfffffffe or NO_VAL).

results.prompt: What does sbatch --parsable return and why is it useful?
results.agent_response:
sbatch --parsable makes sbatch emit a single machine-readable token (the assigned Slurm job id information) instead of the human-readable line ("Submitted batch job 12345"). For plain submissions that token is the job id; for array submissions it contains the job/array identifiers in a compact, parseable form.

Why it’s useful
- easy to capture in scripts: JOBID=$(sbatch --parsable job.sh)
- safe to feed to other Slurm commands (scancel, squeue, scontrol, or sbatch --dependency=afterok:$JOBID) without brittle text parsing
- avoids locale/human-message changes and extra text that break automation

Example (script-friendly): 
JOBID=$(sbatch --parsable my_job.sh)
squeue -j "$JOBID"

results.prompt: Explain Slurm exit code and derived exit code fields from accounting
results.agent_response:
Short summary (what each field is and how to read it)

- ExitCode
  - The ExitCode field is the exit status captured for the job (or job step) and is shown in the form exit:signal (for example the docs show 0:0). The left value is the 8‑bit exit/return code, the right value is a terminating signal number when a signal caused termination.
  - Which value is captured:
    - sbatch: the return code of the batch script.
    - srun: the return code of the command run by srun (each step records its own ExitCode).
    - salloc: the return value that terminates the salloc session.
  - Semantics:
    - Exit codes are treated as unsigned 8‑bit (0–255); negative returns are displayed as their unsigned representation.
    - Any non‑zero exit code is treated as a failure and will produce a job state FAILED with reason NonZeroExitCode (unless another failure condition overrides it).

- DerivedExitCode (and the job comment)
  - The DerivedExitCode is a derived/DB field stored with the job record (and an associated comment string). It is initially set by Slurm to the highest exit code returned by the job’s steps (so it reflects step-level failures even when the top-level script returns 0).
  - The DerivedExitCode is maintained by the controller and written to the accounting DB when AccountingStorage is enabled.
  - Administrators can inspect and change the DerivedExitCode and comment with sjobexitmod (the docs show usage and examples where a job’s DerivedExitCode becomes 49:0 with a comment like "out of memory").
  - sacct can display both ExitCode and DerivedExitCode via --format.

Why both exist (practical note)
- ExitCode shows what a specific job entry or step returned; DerivedExitCode gives a concise, DB-level summary of the worst step failure for the whole job (useful when a batch script exits 0 but one of several srun steps failed). The comment field can carry a human explanation that admins or users add.

References (documented behavior)
- Slurm job exit code docs (job_exit_code) describe the exit:signal format, 8‑bit range, step exit capture, DerivedExitCode initialization, and sjobexitmod for modification.
- sacct supports showing ExitCode and DerivedExitCode in accounting output.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

# Job Reason Codes
These reason codes can be used to identify why a pending job has not yet been
started by the scheduler. There may be multiple reasons why a job cannot start,

results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer first: there is no official job-reason named "QOSMaxJobsPerUser" in the Slurm job-reason list. QOS job-count limits are implemented with QOS attributes (MaxJobs / MaxSubmitJobs / GrpJobs / active_jobs in the REST API, etc.) and when those limits block a job the scheduler reports one of the standard association/limit reason codes (for example AssociationJobLimit, AssocGrp*, AssocMax*, Max*PerAccount). The QOS may also use the DenyOnLimit flag to reject jobs at submission instead of letting them pend.

What the pieces mean and how they map to pending reasons
- QOS limits (where you set them with sacctmgr show/modify qos) can include:
  - MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs (job-count style limits),
  - GrpJobs (group/aggregate job-count),
  - GrpTRES / MaxTRES (aggregate resource caps),
  - other Max* or Grp* limits (per-node, per-account TRES, wall time, nodes, …),
  - Flags such as DenyOnLimit or OverPartQOS.
  (The REST API exposes similar fields such as jobs and active_jobs for a QOS.)
- Enforcement and precedence:
  - Limits are applied in the documented hierarchy (Partition QOS, Job QOS, user association, account association, cluster, partition). A limit defined earlier in the precedence chain wins.
  - If the QOS has DenyOnLimit set, jobs that would exceed a QOS 'Max' limit are denied at submission (rejected) rather than queued.
- How those limits show up as squeue/scontrol reasons:
  - AssociationJobLimit — the job's association has reached its maximum job count (common when a per-user/per-account job-count limit is active).
  - AssocGrp* — an aggregate/group limit (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.) has been reached.
  - AssocMax* / AssocMax…Limit / Max*PerAccount — a requested value exceeds a defined maximum for the association/QOS (the job would violate a Max limit).
  - Max*PerAccount (or Max*PerUser variants shown by some installs) appear when a per-account/per-user maximum (on TRES, jobs, nodes, etc.) is violated.
  - (The job_reason_codes documentation lists all reason-code names and short descriptions — use that to match the reason string you see.)
- Important behavior notes:
  - If a QOS limit only becomes true when considering multiple jobs together (group limits), affected jobs will pend with a group/association reason (not necessarily a QOS-named reason).
  - Only the single reason encountered by the attempted scheduling method is shown; other applicable limits may also exist but are not displayed.

How to diagnose a job pending for a QOS limit
- First look at the queue reason: squeue (the pending Reason column) for the job ID.
- If you need more detail: scontrol show job <JOBID> will show the job's QOS, association, and any limit-related fields the scheduler considered.
- Inspect configured limits:
  - sacctmgr show qos format=... (or sacctmgr show qos) to view the QOS attributes (MaxJobs, GrpJobs, DenyOnLimit, …).
  - sacctmgr show assoc user=<user> (or account=<acct>) to see user/account association limits that may override/augment the QOS.
- If a job was rejected at submission, check sbatch/srun error text and whether the QOS has DenyOnLimit enabled.

If you want, tell me a specific job ID (or show the squeue Reason line) and I can walk through the exact mapping and the sacctmgr/scontrol queries to find which configured limit is blocking it.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None

the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.

- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

following limits: Max[Time|Wall], [Min|Max]Nodes. For these limits, even

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

# Quality of Service (QOS)
One can specify a Quality of Service (QOS) for each job submitted
to Slurm. The QOSs are defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr
command. Jobs request a QOS using the "--qos=" option to the
sbatch , salloc , and srun commands.

## QOS examples[#examples](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
QOS manipulation examples. All QOS operations are done using
the sacctmgr command. The default output of 'sacctmgr show qos' is
very long given the large number of limits and options available
so it is best to use the format option which filters the display.
By default when a cluster is added to the database a default
qos named normal is created.
```text
$ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0
```
Add a new QOS
```text
$ sacctmgr add qos zebra Adding QOS(s) zebra Settings Description = QOS Name $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 0
```
Set QOS priority
```text
$ sacctmgr modify qos zebra set priority=10 Modified qos... zebra $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 10
```
Set some other limits
```text
$ sacctmgr modify qos z...

results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- QOS MaxJobsPerUser is a QOS-enforced limit that restricts how many jobs a single user may have under that QOS. When a job would exceed a configured QOS limit the scheduler will either pend the job with a reason that indicates which limit was hit or (if the QOS has Flags=DenyOnLimit) reject it at submission.
- The pending reason you see in squeue/sview identifies which specific limit blocked the job (e.g., a per-user job count limit, a per-account TRES limit, submit-count limits, etc.). Use squeue (reason column) and scontrol show job <id> to see the exact reason for a pending job.

What MaxJobsPerUser means (and related QOS limits)
- MaxJobs, MaxJobsPerUser (per-user job counts) — limit the number of jobs allowed. If the QOS sets a MaxJobsPerUser (or the association has an equivalent per-user limit), a new job that would make that user exceed the limit will not be started.
- MaxSubmitJobs — controls how many jobs the association/QOS will allow to be submitted (queued) for a user; exceeding it can block submission or cause pending behavior depending on flags.
- MaxTRES / GrpTRES / MaxTRESPerNode / related TRES limits — resource-count limits (CPUs, GPUs, memory) applied per-QOS or per-association; hitting these yields a TRES-related pending reason.
- MaxWall / MaxTime / Min/MaxNodes — other Max* limits that can cause pending reasons when job requests exceed allowed sizes/time.

How that shows up as pending reasons
- The scheduler maps a violated limit to a reason code shown in squeue (or sview). Examples of the kinds of reason you will see:
  - a per-QOS/per-account/per-user job-count limit (MaxJobs or MaxJobsPerUser) → a MaxJobs-type reason
  - submit-count limits (MaxSubmitJobs) → a MaxSubmitJobs/submit-limit reason
  - TRES (CPU/GPU/mem) limits → MaxTRES* or AssocGrp*/AssocMax* style reasons
  - group/association aggregate limits → AssocGrp* reasons
- Only the single reason encountered by the scheduling method is shown. If multiple limits would block the job, only the first-check reason is displayed.

Important behaviors to know
- Limit precedence: Slurm evaluates limits in a hierarchy (Partition QOS, Job QOS, user association, account associations up the chain, cluster). The first level where a limit is defined is the limit that will apply.
- DenyOnLimit flag: If a QOS has Flags=DenyOnLimit, jobs violating that QOS’s Max limits will be denied at submission rather than queued and pending. If DenyOnLimit is not set, jobs that would exceed the limit will typically pend until resources/quotas free up.
- Group (Grp*) limits: Group or association aggregate limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES) are checked when a job is considered for allocation; if starting a job would exceed a group aggregate, it will be blocked and show the corresponding AssocGrp* reason.
- Relative QOS: In newer Slurm versions a QOS can use Flags=Relative so Max limits are interpreted as percentages of cluster resources — the same reason semantics apply, but the value calculation differs.

How to diagnose a job pending for QOS limits
- squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %R" (or use sview) — check the REASON column for the pending job.
- scontrol show job <jobid> — get the job’s QOS, QOS limits in effect, and additional fields.
- sacctmgr show qos format=... or sacctmgr show association / sacctmgr show user — inspect the QOS and association limits (MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, GrpTRES, Flags like DenyOnLimit).
- If you see a MaxJobs/MaxSubmitJobs/TRES-related reason, inspect how many jobs or resources the user/account currently has (squeue, sshare) to determine what’s consuming the quota.

Example troubleshooting steps
1. squeue -j <jobid>  -> note the REASON and the QOS used by the job.
2. scontrol show job <jobid> -> confirm job QOS and requested resources.
3. sacctmgr show qos <qosname> format=name,flags,maxjobs,maxsubmitjobs,max_tres,... -> see configured QOS limits and whether DenyOnLimit is set.
4. squeue -u <user> (and sshare) -> count the user’s running/pending jobs and current usage to compare against limits.

How to change limits (admin)
- Use sacctmgr to modify QOS or association limits (sacctmgr modify qos <name> set MaxJobs=..., set Flags=DenyOnLimit, etc.). Because QOS limits override association limits, be sure you understand the hierarchy before changing values.

References
- Slurm documentation: QOS and Resource Limits pages (explain QOS limits, Flags=DenyOnLimit, and the precedence order) and the Job Reason Codes page (lists the reason strings used by squeue).

If you want, tell me a job ID that is pending for you and I can show the exact squeue reason and the QOS/association limits (I will run squeue and scontrol show job as needed).

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## System Administration [#administration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A new configuration parameter has been added to control the maximum
job array size: MaxArraySize . The smallest index that can be specified
by a user is zero and the maximum index is MaxArraySize minus one.
The default value of MaxArraySize is 1001.
The maximum MaxArraySize supported in Slurm is 4000001.
Be mindful about the value of MaxArraySize as job arrays offer an easy way
for users to submit large numbers of jobs very quickly.
The sched/backfill plugin has been modified to improve performance with
job arrays. Once one element of a job array is discovered to not be runnable
or impact the scheduling of pending jobs, the remaining elements of that job
array will be quickly skipped.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit

Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)

defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The
QOS will only influence job scheduling priority when the multi-factor
priority plugin is loaded and a non-zero "PriorityWeightQOS" has been
defined in the slurm.conf file. The QOS will only determine job
preemption when the "PreemptType" is defined as "preempt/qos" in the
slurm.conf file. Limits defined for a QOS (and described above) will
override the limits of the user/account/cluster/partition
association.

## Coordinator[#coord](https://slurm.schedmd.com/user_permissions.html)
A special privileged user, usually an account manager, that can add
users or sub-accounts to the account they are coordinator over.
This should be a trusted person since they can change limits on account and
user associations, as well as cancel, requeue or reassign accounts of jobs
inside their realm. Note that a coordinator may not increase job limits above
the parent ones.
Set using a table in Slurm's database defining users and accounts for
which they can serve as coordinators.
For configuration information, see the
[sacctmgr](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html) man page.

defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

QOS manipulation examples. All QOS operations are done using
the sacctmgr command. The default output of 'sacctmgr show qos' is

The partition configuration permits you to establish different job
limits or access controls for various groups (or partitions) of nodes.

slurm.conf is an ASCII file which describes general Slurm
configuration information, the nodes to be managed, information about

## System Administration [#administration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A new configuration parameter has been added to control the maximum
job array size: MaxArraySize . The smallest index that can be specified
by a user is zero and the maximum index is MaxArraySize minus one.
The default value of MaxArraySize is 1001.
The maximum MaxArraySize supported in Slurm is 4000001.
Be mindful about the value of MaxArraySize as job arrays offer an easy way
for users to submit large numbers of jobs very quickly.
The sched/backfill plugin has been modified to improve performance with
job arrays. Once one element of a job array is discovered to not be runnable
or impact the scheduling of pending jobs, the remaining elements of that job
array will be quickly skipped.

results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
Summary
- QOS MaxJobsPerUser is a QOS-level limit that caps how many jobs a single user may have under that QOS. When the limit is hit, additional jobs that would violate it will not be scheduled and will show a pending reason tied to the QOS limit (commonly displayed as QOSMaxJobsPerUser).
- A QOS can either cause jobs to pend when limits are hit, or if the QOS has the DenyOnLimit flag set, new submissions that would violate the limit are rejected at submission time instead of being queued.

What QOSMaxJobsPerUser means (behavior)
- The MaxJobsPerUser value on a QOS restricts the number of jobs a single user can have counted toward that QOS. When a user already has that many jobs, any further job that would exceed the limit becomes ineligible for scheduling.
- The scheduler reports the specific reason (for example, QOSMaxJobsPerUser) so you can identify the limit being enforced.
- QOS limits override the same types of limits set on the user/account association (the QOS limits take precedence).

Related pending/reason codes you will see and how to interpret them
- QOSMaxJobsPerUser — the QOS MaxJobsPerUser limit is preventing the job from being scheduled.
- Max*PerAccount / QOSMax* / AssocMax* / AssocGrp* — groupings of reason codes you may encounter when other association- or account-level limits are hit (these are the family names used in the Slurm job reason list). For example, a “Max…PerAccount” reason means a per-account/QOS maximum was exceeded.
- DenyOnLimit (QOS flag) — not a pending reason itself but changes behavior: when set the job will be rejected at submit time rather than queued and shown with a pending reason.

How to investigate a job stuck for this reason
- See the scheduler’s reported pending reason: squeue (the REASON column will show the code such as QOSMaxJobsPerUser).
- For a single job, get the detailed reason: scontrol show job <jobid>.
- Inspect QOS limits (and DenyOnLimit): sacctmgr show qos (or sacctmgr show qos format=... to list specific fields).
- Inspect association/account limits if the reason indicates an association-level limit: sacctmgr show association or sacctmgr show account.

How to remedy or change behavior
- If the limit is appropriate but you need more capacity for a user, increase MaxJobsPerUser on the QOS: sacctmgr modify qos <qosname> set MaxJobsPerUser=<N>
- If you prefer submissions to be rejected instead of queued when limits are exceeded, enable DenyOnLimit on the QOS: sacctmgr modify qos <qosname> set DenyOnLimit=1
- If the limit should be applied differently, consider changing which QOS the job uses, adjusting association/account limits, or increasing the cluster resources available to that QOS.

Notes and troubleshooting tips
- The REASON reported by squeue is the single reason encountered by the scheduler at the time it tried to schedule the job; multiple limits may apply but only one reason is shown.
- QOS limits take precedence over association limits when both exist for the job.
- Exact command output and field names can vary by Slurm version; use scontrol and sacctmgr on your controller to see the precise configured values.

If you want, I can check the live queue or a specific job’s pending reason (squeue / scontrol show job), or list QOS settings on your cluster (sacctmgr show qos). Which job ID or QOS name should I inspect?

results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- A QOS "Max jobs per user" limit (set via the QOS Max* limits in the Slurm DB) constrains how many jobs a single user may have under that QOS/association. When that limit is reached, new jobs that would violate it are either pended by the scheduler or rejected at submission depending on the QOS flags.

What the limit actually does
- MaxJobsPerUser (and related Max* limits) are enforced when the scheduler evaluates whether a job may start or be allowed to exist concurrently. The check is applied against the appropriate scope (QOS first if set there, otherwise the association/partition/cluster limits per the hierarchy).
- If a job would violate the limit:
  - If the QOS has the DenyOnLimit flag set, the job will be denied at submission (sbatch fails).
  - If DenyOnLimit is not set, the job is allowed to be submitted but will pend until the limiting condition clears.

How this appears in squeue (pending reasons)
- The scheduler places a short reason string in the squeue "REASON" (or NODELIST(REASON)) column to indicate why a job is pending. Limit-related reasons follow recognizable patterns:
  - Reasons that mention the association or group (Assoc*, Association*) indicate association-level aggregate limits.
  - Reasons that mention Max*/PerUser or Max*/PerAccount indicate a per-user or per-account maximum was hit.
  - If a QOS limit is the cause you will see a reason that points to a QOS/Max limit (the exact token depends on your Slurm build/version and the specific limit; common patterns are QOSMax* or Max*PerUser/PerAccount or AssocMax*).
- Because squeue shows only the reason the scheduler encountered during its attempt, multiple limits might apply but only the first-matched reason is shown.

How to diagnose which limit was hit
- Look at the job’s REASON in squeue first to see the short code the scheduler returned.
- For a specific job id, run scontrol show job <jobid> to see detailed fields (AllocTRES, associations, QOS used) and sometimes more detail about limits applied.
- Inspect QOS and association limits with sacctmgr:
  - sacctmgr show qos
  - sacctmgr show assoc user=<user> or sacctmgr show assoc account=<account>
These show any MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, MaxTRESPerUser, etc., that might be blocking the job.

Common related limits you may run into
- MaxJobs (per QOS/association/partition) — caps concurrent jobs.
- MaxSubmitJobs — caps how many jobs a user may have submitted (affects new submissions).
- MaxTRESPerUser / MaxTRESPERACCOUNT — caps on TRES (CPUs, GPUs, etc.) per user/account.
- Grp* limits — aggregate limits applied across an association/group that can also cause pending reasons.

Behavioral notes and tips
- Hierarchy: Partition-QOS limits are evaluated before job-QOS/association limits unless you set OverPartQOS. This can lead to a partition-level limit appearing to block jobs even if the job’s QOS appears to allow them.
- If you want jobs to be rejected at submit time rather than queued and pended, enable the QOS DenyOnLimit flag for that QOS.
- To unblock/presume jobs: increase the appropriate Max* limit in the QOS or association, change the job’s QOS (if allowed), or free running jobs that count against the limit.
- Use squeue -o with the REASON field (or scontrol show job) to get the exact text that your cluster will display so you can map it to the specific limit.

Example commands (admin)
- View QOS settings: sacctmgr show qos format=Name,MaxJobs,MaxSubmitJobs,DenyOnLimit
- View associations for a user: sacctmgr show assoc user=<user> with detail
- Change a QOS limit: sacctmgr modify qos <qosname> set MaxJobs=<n>
- Toggle deny: sacctmgr modify qos <qosname> set DenyOnLimit=YES|NO

If you tell me a concrete job ID or paste the REASON text you see in squeue, I can explain exactly which limit type that reason corresponds to and suggest the minimal change to fix it.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.

results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- QOSMaxJobsPerUser (commonly configured as the QOS field MaxJobsPerUser) is a per-QOS limit that caps how many jobs a single user may have simultaneously under that QOS. It is enforced by the scheduler when evaluating pending jobs.
- When a job would exceed such a limit the scheduler will either pend the job (and assign a pending reason that identifies the violated limit) or—if the QOS has the DenyOnLimit flag—deny the job at submission.

Details and what to expect
- Purpose: MaxJobsPerUser prevents one user from owning more than N concurrent jobs in that QOS. It is set in the Slurm database (sacctmgr) on the QOS record.
- Enforcement behavior:
  - By default a job that would breach a Max* limit will pend until resources/slots become available.
  - If the QOS has DenyOnLimit set, jobs that would violate the QOS Max limits are rejected at submission instead of pending.
  - Limits are applied using Slurm’s hierarchy (partition QOS limits may be applied before the job’s requested QOS unless OverPartQOS is set). See resource-limits documentation for the full precedence order.
- Pending reasons shown by the scheduler:
  - When the scheduler evaluates a pending job and finds it violates a configured resource/association limit, it assigns a job reason describing the limit that was hit. The job reason page documents families such as AssocMax* (association maximums) and Max*PerAccount (per-account-per-QOS maximums).
  - In practice a job blocked by a per-user-per-QOS limit will show a reason that maps to the exceeded limit (examples in the docs include AssocMax* and Max*PerAccount-style reason codes). If DenyOnLimit is in effect the job is rejected instead of receiving a pending reason.
- How to diagnose a job stuck by a QOS limit:
  - Use squeue (include the Reason/REASON column) to see the scheduler’s short pending reason for active queue entries.
  - If squeue’s output doesn’t give enough detail, run scontrol show job <jobid> to get the detailed evaluation/limit fields.
- How to change the behavior:
  - Adjust the QOS with sacctmgr, e.g. sacctmgr modify qos <qosname> set MaxJobsPerUser=<N> (or remove/alter DenyOnLimit / OverPartQOS as needed).
  - Remember limits can also be defined at user/account/cluster/partition levels; the first-defined limit in the configured hierarchy is the one applied.

References (Slurm docs)
- Resource limits and QOS behavior (Max* limits, DenyOnLimit, OverPartQOS)
- Job reason codes (lists the reason families such as AssocMax* and Max*PerAccount)
These documents explain the exact reason strings the scheduler will use and the limit-precedence rules.

results.prompt: Explain AssocGrpGRES and association group resource limits
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" is the association/group-level GRES (Generic RESource) limit entry shown in sacctmgr/association listings. It represents limits on GRES usage (for example GPUs) that apply to the association (user/account/cluster/partition association) when Slurm evaluates whether a pending job may be allocated resources.

What association (group) resource limits do
- Association limits are per-association attributes maintained with sacctmgr and tested at job allocation time. Example group limits include GrpJobs, GrpTRES (trackable resources), and GRES-specific limits.
- If starting a job would cause any group limit to be exceeded, that job will not be considered for scheduling (it will remain pending). Group limits are enforced before attempting allocation; a job will not be started simply because it could preempt others to satisfy the limit.
- Limits are hierarchical. When multiple limits exist the precedence is: job QOS/partition QOS ordering rules, then user association, account association(s), cluster/root association, then partition-level limits (the first place a limit is defined is used).

Important GRES-specific behavior and pitfalls
- GRES limits are expressed as TRES entries (e.g. gres/gpu) or in higher-level fields such as GrpTRES. You can set limits addressing a specific GRES type (for example MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1).
- Type-specific limits have a design limitation: if a user requests a generic GRES (for example --gres=gpu:2) a limit set on a specific type (gres/gpu:tesla) will not be enforced. In other words, type-scoped limits do not prevent a user from requesting an untyped generic GRES and receiving two devices of that type unless additional submit-time checking is enforced (for example via a Lua job_submit plugin).
- TRES limit modifications using "+=" or "-=" are supported; attempting to set a negative value will set the TRES to zero. Large numeric bounds are handled up to the internal limit noted in the docs.

Operational effects of changing associations/limits
- Changes made with sacctmgr are uploaded to the controllers and take effect immediately for scheduling decisions.
- Deleting an association will immediately cancel running or pending jobs that belong to that association.
- Lowering a limit does not retroactively kill running jobs to satisfy the new limit; it only affects future allocation decisions.

Where to view and manage them
- Use sacctmgr to list and modify associations and their limits (association records contain fields for GrpTRES/GrpJobs/MaxTRESPerUser and related attributes).
- The Slurm resource_limits documentation describes the precedence, semantics, and example formats; the gres documentation describes GRES configuration and limitations.
