results.prompt: Explain AssocGrpGRES and association group resource limits
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" is an accounting/association-level concept for GRES (generic resources, e.g., GPUs) that appears in the association/group resource limits exposed by Slurm accounting (sacctmgr/sacct). It expresses the group-level GRES/TRES limits or usage that apply to an association (the association is the combination of user/account/cluster/partition).
- Association/group GRES limits are enforced at job allocation time: if starting a job would cause any group limit to be exceeded, that job will not be considered for scheduling. Limits are applied according to Slurm’s association/limit hierarchy (QOS/partition → job QOS → user association → account association(s) → cluster, etc.).
- GRES limits can be expressed using TRES syntax (examples: gres/gpu=2 or gres/gpu:tesla=1). A notable caveat: a type-specific limit (for example MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1) does not prevent a user from requesting a generic --gres=gpu:2 and thereby obtaining two of that model; enforcing that requires a job_submit plugin or forcing users to request specific types.

Key behavior and admin notes
- Which fields control these limits: association/group-level fields such as GrpTRES (and other Grp* fields like GrpJobs) are used to limit aggregate resources for an association. These are evaluated when the scheduler considers a job for allocation.
- Enforcement prerequisites and effects:
  - AccountingStorageEnforce must include limits (i.e., AccountingStorageEnforce=limits) in slurm.conf for Slurm to enforce association limits.
  - When limits are lowered, running jobs are not retroactively killed to satisfy the new lower limits; new/queued jobs are blocked if they would exceed the lowered limits.
  - Deleting an association will cancel running or pending jobs that belong to that association immediately.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
Summary
- A "hold" prevents a job from being considered for scheduling; held jobs remain in PENDING and will not be allocated resources even if dependencies, reservation, or resources would otherwise allow them to run.
- Releasing a hold makes the job eligible again; once released, normal scheduling rules (priority, backfill, dependencies, reservations) determine when it actually runs.

How to set/remove holds
- Submit-time: sbatch --hold will submit the job on hold (it starts PENDING/held).
- Ad-hoc: scontrol hold <jobid> (or scontrol hold jobid=<id>) sets a hold; scontrol release <jobid> removes it.
- There are multiple hold-types (user/admin/system/etc.) with different authorization levels; the exact command forms and options are scontrol hold/release and sbatch --hold.

Who can set and who can clear
- Job owner (unprivileged user): may place and clear USER-type holds on their own jobs.
- Privileged users / administrators (Operator/Administrator): can place and clear ADMIN/SYSTEM and other privileged hold types on any job.
- If multiple holds (different types) exist on a job, all active holds must be cleared before the job becomes eligible to run. Clearing only one hold type is not sufficient if another hold remains.

Visible effects and diagnostics
- Held jobs show as PENDING (PD) in squeue; the REASON/StateReason or scontrol show job output indicates a hold (e.g., JobHeld / Hold flags).
- scontrol show job <id> provides the detailed hold flags and reasons.
- Holds do not consume compute resources while the job is waiting.

Interactions and important notes
- Holds override satisfied dependencies and reservations: a job will remain held even if its dependencies are met.
- Holds apply to the job-level allocation (and therefore affect job steps). For arrays or heterogeneous jobs you can target whole job or specific array elements when using job identifiers that include indices.
- Holds are distinct from suspend/requeue: use suspend/requeue to stop or move a running job; holds are primarily a PENDING-state control.
- Authorization matters: an owner cannot clear an ADMIN or SYSTEM hold set by administrators; admins can clear owner-type holds as well.

Quick examples
- Submit held: sbatch --hold myscript.sh
- Place a hold: scontrol hold jobid=12345
- Remove a hold: scontrol release jobid=12345
- Inspect hold flags: scontrol show job 12345 (look for Hold= / StateReason / JobState)

If you want, I can show the exact hold flags and the REASON text by running squeue / scontrol show job on a specific job ID — tell me which job ID to inspect.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
Summary — what a hold does
- A hold prevents a job from being initiated by the scheduler. Held jobs remain in PENDING and will not be allocated resources until the hold(s) preventing them are removed.
- Holds affect job eligibility only; they do not terminate or change the runtime of an already RUNNING job (use suspend/requeue/cancel to affect running tasks).

Common hold types (what you’ll see in Slurm)
- UserHold: placed by the submitting user (or by scontrol when invoked by that user). Shows as a user-caused hold reason.
- AdminHold: placed by an administrator. Normal users cannot create AdminHold and generally cannot clear it.
- SystemHold: placed by Slurm/system (for example, due to a system condition). Only privileged/system actions clear it.
- A job’s Hold field may list more than one hold type; the job will not run until every active hold is cleared.

How holds are applied and removed
- Submission-time hold: sbatch --hold submits the job in held state.
- Post-submission: scontrol hold JobId=<id> (or the equivalent UI) places a hold. scontrol release JobId=<id> removes hold(s).
- Permissions: who can set/release which holds depends on privileges — users can generally set/release their own UserHold, admins can set/release AdminHold and clear other holds, SystemHold is managed by Slurm/system.
- Releasing: removing all active holds makes the job eligible for scheduling; if resources/priority permit, the scheduler can start it immediately.

Interactions and special cases
- Multiple holds stack: if any hold remains, the job stays pending.
- Job arrays: operations given the array JobID act on the whole array unless an element is explicitly targeted.
- Dependencies / StartTime: a hold is another gating condition. Even after release, other constraints (dependencies, BeginTime, resource limits, QOS/reservation restrictions) can keep the job pending.
- Visibility: squeue will typically show the pending reason (e.g., "UserHold" or "AdminHold"); scontrol show job shows detailed Hold and other fields.
- Holding a running job: placing a hold does not automatically suspend/stop an already running job. Use scontrol suspend / scontrol requeue / scancel for running-job control.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
Summary
- A "hold" prevents a job from being allocated/run; the job remains in the queue (typically in PENDING) and will not be scheduled until all active holds on it are removed.
- Holds are additive: a job can have multiple hold types at once. Removing one hold does not schedule the job if any other hold remains (or other scheduling constraints still block it).

Hold types and semantics
- UserHold
  - Intended for the job owner (or a user with appropriate privileges).
  - Commonly placed at submission time with sbatch --hold or later by the job owner (or by an admin acting on behalf).
  - The job owner (and admins) can release a UserHold.
- AdminHold
  - Set by administrators (e.g., site policy or manual admin intervention).
  - Ordinary users cannot remove an AdminHold; only admins can release it.
- SystemHold
  - Placed by Slurm/system components for system-level reasons (maintenance, controller action, etc.).
  - Typically cleared by the system or by administrators when the underlying condition is resolved.

Commands and inspection
- Place a hold:
  - sbatch --hold (submit job in held state)
  - scontrol hold <jobid> (place a hold on an existing job)
- Clear a hold:
  - scontrol release <jobid> (release holds; permission rules apply — admins can clear Admin/System holds; owners can clear UserHold)
- Inspect hold/state:
  - squeue shows job state and often a reason column (held jobs display a hold-related reason).
  - scontrol show job <jobid> gives detailed job fields (including hold info).
- Job arrays and components:
  - scontrol operations on an ArrayJobID apply to all elements by default; you can target individual elements with the element-specific jobid (ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID).

Behavioral notes / interactions
- Holds prevent scheduling even if resources are available and any dependencies are satisfied. Releasing the hold only makes the job eligible again; it may still remain pending for other reasons (resources, dependencies, QOS limits, reservations, etc.).
- Holds do not terminate or cancel a job. A held job stays in the queue until released or explicitly cancelled.
- Holding a running job is not the same as suspending it; to stop a running job you would use job suspension/requeue mechanisms (scontrol suspend/requeue), not a hold.
- Permissions matter: who can set/release which hold type follows the Owner vs Admin vs System separation; admins have broader authority.

Practical tips
- Use sbatch --hold if you want a job submitted but prevent it from starting until you explicitly release it.
- Use scontrol show job and squeue to confirm which hold type(s) are present and why a job is not starting.
- If a job remains pending after release, check resource availability, dependencies, partition/reservation constraints, and QOS/limits.

Commands referenced
- sbatch --hold
- scontrol hold <jobid>
- scontrol release <jobid>
- squeue
- scontrol show job <jobid>

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:

to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill

nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## SIGNALS AND ESCAPE SEQUENCES[#SECTION_SIGNALS-AND-ESCAPE-SEQUENCES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
Signals sent to the srun command are automatically forwarded to
the tasks it is controlling with a few exceptions. The escape sequence
<control-c> will report the state of all tasks associated with
the srun command. If <control-c> is entered twice within
one second, then the associated SIGINT signal will be sent to all tasks
and a termination sequence will be entered sending SIGCONT, SIGTERM,
and SIGKILL to all spawned tasks.
If a third <control-c> is received, the srun program will be
terminated without waiting for remote tasks to exit or their I/O to
complete.
The escape sequence <control-z> is presently ignored.

### Valid and Invalid Requests [#Valid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request
`c>=0.00000001` is fulfilled.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

%J [#OPT_%J](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) jobid.stepid of the running job (e.g. "128.0"). The stepid is only expanded for
regular steps, not for special steps like "batch" or "extern".

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```

```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

### Valid and Invalid Requests [#Valid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request
`c>=0.00000001` is fulfilled.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

### Valid and Invalid Requests [#Valid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request
`c>=0.00000001` is fulfilled.

## SIGNALS AND ESCAPE SEQUENCES[#SECTION_SIGNALS-AND-ESCAPE-SEQUENCES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
Signals sent to the srun command are automatically forwarded to
the tasks it is controlling with a few exceptions. The escape sequence
<control-c> will report the state of all tasks associated with
the srun command. If <control-c> is entered twice within
one second, then the associated SIGINT signal will be sent to all tasks
and a termination sequence will be entered sending SIGCONT, SIGTERM,
and SIGKILL to all spawned tasks.
If a third <control-c> is received, the srun program will be
terminated without waiting for remote tasks to exit or their I/O to
complete.
The escape sequence <control-z> is presently ignored.

### Valid and Invalid Requests [#Valid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request
`c>=0.00000001` is fulfilled.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```

```text

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Submitting Jobs [#submitting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The salloc , sbatch and srun commands can all be used
to submit heterogeneous jobs.
Resource specifications for each component of the heterogeneous job should be
separated with ":" character.
For example:
```text
$ sbatch --cpus-per-task=4 --mem-per-cpu=1 --ntasks=128 : \ --cpus-per-task=1 --mem-per-cpu=16 --ntasks=1 my.bash
```
Options specified for one component of a heterogeneous job (or job step) will
be used for subsequent components to the extent which is expected to be helpful.
Propagated options can be reset as desired for each component (e.g. a different
account name could be specified for each hetjob component.
For example, --immediate and --job-name are propagated, while
--ntasks and --mem-per-cpu are reset to default values for each
component.
A list of propagated options follows.
- --account
- --acctg-freq
- --begin
- --cluster-constraint

results.prompt: Explain Slurm --constraint syntax for node features
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Use -C or --constraint to select nodes by their configured Feature tokens (the Feature= list on each NodeName in slurm.conf).
- The constraint value is a boolean expression of feature names; use & (AND) or comma (,) for AND, | for OR, and parentheses to group. Quote the expression so the shell doesn’t split it.

Details and examples
- Features: Nodes are tagged in slurm.conf (or helpers.conf) with Feature=token1,token2,...; --constraint matches those tokens.
- Operators:
  - & or , — logical AND (both features must be present)
  - | — logical OR (one or the other)
  - ( ) — grouping/precedence
- Quoting: put the whole expression in quotes, e.g. -C "gpu&v100" or -C "(gpu|fpga),ssd".
- Examples:
  - -C "v100" — any node with feature v100
  - -C "gpu|fpga" — nodes with gpu OR fpga
  - -C "gpu,ssd" (or -C "gpu&ssd") — nodes that have both gpu AND ssd
  - -C "(gpu|fpga),highmem" — nodes that are highmem AND either gpu or fpga

Notes
- --constraint matches the feature tokens assigned to nodes; it filters at job submission time.
- There is a separate "extra constraints" mechanism (SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints) with its own key/value syntax if your site uses node Extra fields rather than Feature tokens.

Snippet:
### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

### Valid and Invalid Requests [#Valid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```

must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request
`c>=0.00000001` is fulfilled.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

Snippet:
## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

Setting CliFilterPlugins=cli_filter/user_defaults in slurm.conf will
allow users to define their own defaults for jobs submitted from the machine(s)
with the configured file. The plugin looks for the definition file in
`$HOME/.slurm/defaults`. It will read each line as a
`component=value` pair, where `component` is any of the

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Valid and Invalid Requests [#Valid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request
`c>=0.00000001` is fulfilled.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

salloc is used to allocate a Slurm job allocation, which is a set of resources
(nodes), possibly with some set of constraints (e.g. number of processors per
node). When salloc successfully obtains the requested allocation, it then runs
the command specified by the user. Finally, when the user specified command is
complete, salloc relinquishes the job allocation.
The command may be any program the user wishes. Some typical commands are
xterm, a shell script containing srun commands, and srun (see the EXAMPLES

shell.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## SIGNALS AND ESCAPE SEQUENCES[#SECTION_SIGNALS-AND-ESCAPE-SEQUENCES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
Signals sent to the srun command are automatically forwarded to
the tasks it is controlling with a few exceptions. The escape sequence
<control-c> will report the state of all tasks associated with
the srun command. If <control-c> is entered twice within
one second, then the associated SIGINT signal will be sent to all tasks
and a termination sequence will be entered sending SIGCONT, SIGTERM,
and SIGKILL to all spawned tasks.
If a third <control-c> is received, the srun program will be
terminated without waiting for remote tasks to exit or their I/O to
complete.
The escape sequence <control-z> is presently ignored.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

### Valid and Invalid Requests [#Valid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request
`c>=0.00000001` is fulfilled.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.

by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be

below.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

### Valid and Invalid Requests [#Valid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request
`c>=0.00000001` is fulfilled.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
Short version
- A node feature is a boolean tag (an attribute) assigned to a node that describes a capability or property (example: gpu, rtx3090, ib, ssd, highmem).
- When a job requests a feature (typically with --constraint or #SBATCH --constraint), the scheduler filters nodes and will only place the job on nodes whose feature expression evaluates true. If no eligible nodes exist, the job remains pending.
- Features are purely a placement/filter mechanism (unlike GRES/TRES which represent countable resources).

Details and behaviors you should know
1) Where features come from
- Static: Features can be listed in slurm.conf on a NodeName line (Feature=...).
- Dynamic / changeable: NodeFeaturesPlugins (helpers.conf) can report and modify features at runtime. Those plugin-managed features can be “available but not active” (common for cloud/on‑demand nodes) and require activation at allocation or a reboot to change.

2) Active vs available (important for cloud/elastic nodes)
- Features not managed by a NodeFeaturesPlugin are always active.
- For plugin-managed features, a node may advertise a feature as available but it isn’t active while the node is powered down. If a job requests such a feature, the controller can select that node and cause the feature to be activated (power up, run helper, etc.) at allocation time.
- Some feature changes require a reboot; helpers and the configured RebootProgram govern that behavior.

3) How jobs request features (placement syntax and logic)
- Jobs request features with --constraint (sbatch/srun/salloc). The scheduler evaluates the request against node feature sets and only considers nodes that match.
- Boolean expressions are supported so you can combine attributes: AND/OR and parentheses are used to build expressions (e.g., request A AND (B OR C)). Different sites accept the usual symbols (& and |, commas for AND, parentheses) — check your cluster’s exact accepted operators in local docs.
- If no node satisfies the constraint expression, the job stays pending until nodes become eligible.

4) How this affects placement and scheduling
- Feature constraints reduce the pool of eligible nodes; the scheduler’s allocation, backfill and site_factor logic operate only over that reduced pool.
- Requesting narrow or uncommon features can increase queue wait time because fewer nodes match.
- If a requested feature must be activated (cloud/available-but-not-active), allocation may trigger node start/reboot and that latency is part of placement.
- Features do not consume numeric resource counts; they are boolean selectors. For countable resources (GPU count, licenses) use GRES/TRES/License mechanisms.

5) Operational notes for admins/users
- Admins define features on nodes (slurm.conf, helpers.conf/plugins) and should document which features are changeable or cloud-managed.
- Users can combine constraints with other resource requests (CPUs, memory, gres). If you think a job is stuck pending because of a feature, inspect node feature lists (sinfo / scontrol show node) to see which nodes advertise the needed feature and whether it’s active or only available.
- Changing a node’s feature or activating plugin features may require node reboot or helper actions.

Example (conceptual)
- sbatch --constraint="gpu&rtx"  — asks only nodes that advertise both gpu and rtx features.
- If rtx is a plugin-managed feature and nodes with rtx are powered down, the controller may power them up to satisfy the allocation.

If you want, I can show how to list the features currently advertised on your cluster’s nodes (sinfo / scontrol show node) so you can see which features are active vs available.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
To summarize the above, the QOSs and their associated limits are
defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The
QOS will only influence job scheduling priority when the multi-factor
priority plugin is loaded and a non-zero "PriorityWeightQOS" has been
defined in the slurm.conf file. The QOS will only determine job
preemption when the "PreemptType" is defined as "preempt/qos" in the
slurm.conf file. Limits defined for a QOS (and described above) will
override the limits of the user/account/cluster/partition
association.

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.

partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
To summarize the above, the QOSs and their associated limits are
defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The
QOS will only influence job scheduling priority when the multi-factor
priority plugin is loaded and a non-zero "PriorityWeightQOS" has been
defined in the slurm.conf file. The QOS will only determine job
preemption when the "PreemptType" is defined as "preempt/qos" in the
slurm.conf file. Limits defined for a QOS (and described above) will
override the limits of the user/account/cluster/partition
association.

## QOS examples[#examples](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
QOS manipulation examples. All QOS operations are done using
the sacctmgr command. The default output of 'sacctmgr show qos' is
very long given the large number of limits and options available
so it is best to use the format option which filters the display.
By default when a cluster is added to the database a default
qos named normal is created.
```text
$ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0

$ sacctmgr add qos zebra Adding QOS(s) zebra Settings Description = QOS Name $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 0
```

```text
$ sacctmgr modify qos zebra set priority=10 Modified qos... zebra $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 10
```
Set some other limits
```text
$ sacctmgr modify qos z...

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.
However, when a relative QOS is also assigned as a partition QOS, some unique
conditions will apply:

## TRES information[#SECTION_TRES-information](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Trackable RESources (TRES) are used in many QOS or Association limits
(GrpTRES* / MaxTRES*). When setting limits, one or more comma-separated
"TRES=value" assignments can be specified.
Each TRES can be one of the Slurm defaults (e.g., cpu , mem ,
node ), or any defined generic resource. You can see the list of available
resources by running sacctmgr show tres .
Each TRES has a different limit, e.g., "GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G" would
establish 2 different limits: one for 16 CPUs and another for 32 GB of memory.
Setting a new value for a TRES type does not affect any other TRES types that
were previously specified. For example, on the same entity as above, a
subsequent assignment of "GrpTRES=gres/gpu=2" will result in
"GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G,gres/gpu=2" applying to that entity.

A QOS can be created, modified, and deleted with sacctmgr. These
options allow you to set the corresponding attributes or filter on them
when querying for a QOS.
NOTE : The group limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.) are tested when a job is
being considered for being allocated resources.
If starting a job would cause any of its group limit to be exceeded,
that job will not be considered for scheduling even if that job might preempt
other jobs which would release sufficient group resources for the pending
job to be initiated.

"[+|-]=" syntax available for association-based entities.

described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"

results.prompt: Explain squeue format strings for job id, state, user, and reason
results.agent_response:
Brief summary of the squeue format codes you’ll use for those four fields, and how to interpret them:

- %i
  - Field: JOBID
  - Meaning: job id (numeric). Can be width/formatted like "%.6i" to zero-pad / right-justify.

- %u
  - Field: USER
  - Meaning: submitting user name.

- %T (and %t)
  - %T: full/human-readable job state (e.g. PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, CANCELLED).
  - %t: short/state code used in the ST column (compact codes such as PD, R, CG, etc).
  - Use %T when you want the full state name, %t when you want the compact ST column.

- %R
  - Field: NODELIST(REASON)
  - Meaning: for RUNNING jobs this prints the node list; for PENDING (and other non-running) jobs it prints the scheduler reason (often shown in parentheses).
  - This is the common column used when you want to see "why" a job is not starting (the scheduler-provided reason string).

Formatting notes
- squeue accepts printf-style width/precision: e.g. squeue -o "%.6i %.12u %.10T %R"
- You can mix %T (long state) or %t (short state) depending on preferred output compactness.
- If you specifically need only the scheduler “reason” text for pending jobs, use the NODELIST(REASON) column (%R) and interpret non-running rows as containing the reason.

Example format strings (use with squeue -o):
- Compact: squeue -o "%i %u %t %R"
- Verbose state and aligned fields: squeue -o "%.8i %.12u %.12T %R"

results.prompt: Explain squeue format strings for job id, state, user, and reason
results.agent_response:
Briefly — squeue -o uses printf-style format tokens. For the four fields you asked about the common tokens are:

- Job ID
  - Token: %i
  - What it prints: the job's numeric JOBID.
  - Example use: "%.6i" prints the job id in a fixed width (right‑justified) field of 6 characters.

- User
  - Token: %u
  - What it prints: the submitting user's name.
  - You can set width/precision the same way as printf (e.g. "%.10u" or "%-12u" to left‑justify).

- State
  - Tokens: %T (full/state name) and %t (short/state code)
  - %T prints the long state string (e.g., RUNNING, PENDING, COMPLETED).
  - %t prints the short single‑letter code (e.g., R, PD).
  - Use width specifiers to align columns (e.g. "%-10T" to left‑justify a 10‑char state column).

- Reason / NodeList column
  - Token: %R
  - What it prints: for pending jobs this is the scheduler "Reason" string; for running jobs this field typically shows the nodelist (squeue prints node list or reason in the same column).
  - The reason text can be long, so truncate or set a width (e.g. "%.30R").

Putting it together (examples)
- Compact, readable: squeue -o "%i %u %T %R"
- Aligned columns with truncation: squeue -o "%.8i %-12u %-10T %.30R"

Notes
- The -o FORMAT string follows printf semantics for width/precision/alignment.
- Many other tokens exist (job name %j, partition %P, time %M, etc.); consult the squeue manpage (squeue(1)) for the full list.

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_state_codes.html)
In the Slurm code, there are base states and state flags .
Each job has a base state and may have additional state flags set. When using
the [REST API](https://slurm.schedmd.com/rest_quickstart.html), both the base state and current
flag(s) will be returned.
When the [squeue](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html) and [sacct](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
command report a job state, they represent it as a single state. Both will
recognize all base states but not all state flags. If a recognized flag is
present, it will be reported instead of the base state. Refer to the relevant
command documentation for details.

code. The names provided are the string representations that are used in

```text

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html)
Executing squeue sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to squeue to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html)
Executing squeue sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to squeue to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## QOS examples[#examples](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
QOS manipulation examples. All QOS operations are done using
the sacctmgr command. The default output of 'sacctmgr show qos' is
very long given the large number of limits and options available
so it is best to use the format option which filters the display.
By default when a cluster is added to the database a default
qos named normal is created.

$ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_state_codes.html)
In the Slurm code, there are base states and state flags .
Each job has a base state and may have additional state flags set. When using
the [REST API](https://slurm.schedmd.com/rest_quickstart.html), both the base state and current
flag(s) will be returned.

command report a job state, they represent it as a single state. Both will
recognize all base states but not all state flags. If a recognized flag is

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html)
Executing squeue sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to squeue to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Explain squeue format strings for job id, state, user, and reason
results.agent_response:
Short summary of the common squeue format fields you asked about, and how to use them.

Format codes (printf-style) — examples you can pass to squeue -o:
- %i — Job ID. Prints the numeric JOBID (same as the JOBID column). You can add width/precision like "%.6i" to right‑justify/pad to 6 digits.
- %u — User. Prints the job owner’s login name (same as the USER column). Width modifiers (e.g. "%-12u") control alignment/truncation.
- %T and %t — State:
  - %T prints the full, human‑readable state name (e.g., RUNNING, PENDING, COMPLETED).
  - %t prints the short/compact state code used in the ST column (e.g., R, PD, CG). Use whichever form you prefer.
- %R — Reason. Prints the scheduler’s pending reason string (e.g., “Resources”, “Priority”) for jobs that are not yet started. For running jobs this is typically empty. Note: the special column NODELIST(REASON) will show the node list and, for pending jobs, the reason in parentheses.

Other notes:
- You may also use column names instead of percent codes (for example: squeue -o "JOBID USER STATE REASON").
- Format modifiers work like printf: width, left/right alignment, precision (e.g. "%-10u", "%10i", "%.20R").
- If you need the detailed pending reason for a single job beyond what squeue shows, scontrol show job <jobid> provides more fields.

Example usage:
- squeue -o "%i %u %T %R"
- squeue -o "%.8i %-12u %-10T %.30R"
