results.prompt: Explain scontrol update NodeName state drain and resume semantics
results.agent_response:
Summary
- scontrol update NodeName=<nodes> State=DRAIN: marks the node(s) as drained so the scheduler will not allocate any new jobs to them.
- scontrol update NodeName=<nodes> State=RESUME: clears the drain state so the node(s) become eligible for scheduling again (they will accept new jobs when idle).

What "State=DRAIN" actually does
- Prevents new allocations: the scheduler will not place new jobs on the drained node(s).
- Does not immediately kill running jobs: currently running jobs remain and are allowed to run to completion (the drain just prevents future allocations). If you want running jobs removed immediately you must cancel or requeue them (scancel / scontrol requeue) — the node drain command itself does not evict jobs.
- Node remains marked with the drain reason (if given) until an explicit resume/undrain is done or a special system action clears it. You can record why you drained the node with Reason="text":
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=DRAIN Reason="maintenance"
- Some higher-level actions (for example POWER_DOWN_ASAP or an ASAP reboot) will drain the node and may be able to clear the drain state later (e.g., cancel_reboot can undrain a node that was drained for an ASAP reboot).

What "State=RESUME" does
- Clears the DRAIN flag so the node becomes schedulable again. If the node is currently free it will be considered IDLE and will receive new allocations; if it still has running jobs it will remain allocated until those jobs finish, and only accept new jobs once its state permits scheduling.
- Resume does not force jobs to start on the node immediately — it simply returns the node to normal availability for the scheduler.

Related notes and caveats
- Authorization: node state updates are privileged operations (Operator/Administrator).
- Use scontrol show node <node> or sinfo to inspect a node’s current State and Reason.
- There are other node states / update variants (DOWN, POWER_DOWN_ASAP, POWER_DOWN_FORCE, etc.) that have different semantics (e.g., indicate failures or trigger power-management hooks). Don’t confuse DRAIN (prevent scheduling) with DOWN (node considered offline/bad) or power-down states (which may call SuspendProgram).
- If you need an immediate evacuation, you must explicitly cancel/requeue running jobs; draining alone will not do that.
- For documented command syntax and all node-state options see scontrol documentation (scontrol update NodeName=... State=... and the Node specification section).

Examples
- Drain with a reason:
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=DRAIN Reason="kernel upgrade"
- Resume (undrain):
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=RESUME

Use scontrol show node node01 or sinfo to verify the node’s state and the Reason field after performing these actions.

## Manual Power Saving[#manual](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```
`scontrol update` command actions/states of interest:
POWER_DOWN [#POWER_DOWN](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
reached.

Will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol notify: Root, SlurmUser, or direct owner
scontrol write batch_script: Privileged or direct...

results.prompt: Explain scontrol update NodeName state drain and resume semantics
results.agent_response:
Summary — what the commands do
- scontrol update NodeName=<node-list> State=DRAIN[,Reason="..."]
  - Marks the specified node(s) as drained so the scheduler will not place any new allocations there.
  - Running jobs are not automatically preempted by the drain operation; they continue to run to completion (or until separately cancelled/requeued).
  - The node(s) remain in the drained state until an explicit resume/clear is performed.
  - You may supply a Reason string which is recorded and visible in node/reason listings.

- scontrol update NodeName=<node-list> State=RESUME
  - Clears the drain marking and returns the node(s) to normal scheduling eligibility (they will appear idle/allocatable and the scheduler may assign new jobs).
  - Use this to return nodes to service after maintenance.

Key notes and semantics
- Authorization: updating node state requires appropriate administrative privileges (see scontrol docs for required AdminLevel).
- Targets: NodeName accepts single names, ranges (e.g., node[01-10]) or special names (e.g., ALL).
- Drain does not implicitly kill or requeue running jobs; if you need running jobs removed you must cancel/requeue them separately.
- Drain is persistent until cleared with RESUME (or other explicit state changes); it is used for planned maintenance or to prevent new allocations.
- There are related node-state actions for power-saving and automated suspend (examples: POWER_DOWN, POWER_DOWN_ASAP, POWER_DOWN_FORCE) that combine draining semantics with node power management; POWER_DOWN_ASAP in particular will drain the node and then attempt to power it down using the configured SuspendProgram.
- Use sinfo / scontrol show node to confirm the node state and view the recorded reason.

Common examples
- Mark a node for maintenance:
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=DRAIN Reason="maintenance"
- Return a node to service:
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=RESUME

For exact syntax, authorization requirements, and the full list of node state keywords (POWER_DOWN_*, etc.), see the scontrol documentation.

results.prompt: Explain scontrol update NodeName state drain and resume semantics
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- State=drain: marks the node so Slurm will not allocate any new jobs to it. If jobs are currently running the node will be left to finish those jobs; while jobs remain it is reported as DRAINING and once idle it is reported as DRAINED. No new allocations are placed on a drained node.
- State=resume (undrain): clears the drain so the node becomes allocatable again (i.e., it is returned to normal/idle/allocatable state).

Details and related semantics (from the Slurm docs)
- Drain semantics: a drain prevents new work from being scheduled on the node. Running jobs are allowed to complete; during that time the node is shown as DRAINING and after they finish it becomes DRAINED. (Power-save variants such as POWER_DOWN_ASAP combine draining with a subsequent power-down action — POWER_DOWN_ASAP “will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the node.”)
- Resume/undrain: an undrain (resume) operation returns a drained node to normal so it can be allocated again. For nodes drained as part of an ASAP reboot/power-down workflow there are helper commands (for example cancel_reboot) that will undrain and clear the reason if appropriate.
- Reason and persistence: Slurm records a Reason for nodes placed into DOWN/DRAINED states (the configuration and node entries include a Reason field). slurmctld preserves DRAINED and DRAINING node states (and associated Reason) across its checkpoints/restarts.
- Reporting: sinfo and scontrol show node state flags such as DRAINING and DRAINED; these are the indicators schedulers and admins should use to understand node availability.
- What this does NOT do: draining does not forcibly kill running jobs (unless you use a force/other action). Draining only prevents new allocations and allows current work to finish (or be handled separately by admin action).

Typical usage examples (conceptual)
- scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=DRAIN  — request the node be drained (can be combined with a Reason field).
- scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=RESUME — undrain the node so it becomes allocatable.

If you want, I can paste the exact scontrol syntax/fields from the Slurm manpage or show how to include a Reason string.

## Manual Power Saving[#manual](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```
`scontrol update` command actions/states of interest:
POWER_DOWN [#POWER_DOWN](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
reached.
POWER_DOWN_ASAP [#POWER_DOWN_ASAP](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs
will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the
node.

results.prompt: Explain scontrol update NodeName state drain and resume semantics
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- scontrol update NodeName=<node-list> State=DRAIN marks the node(s) so Slurm will not allocate any new jobs on them. Existing running jobs stay untouched and continue to run until they exit (Slurm does not kill or requeue them just because you issued State=DRAIN).
- scontrol update NodeName=<node-list> State=RESUME (or State=resume) clears the drain state so the node(s) become eligible for new allocations again (subject to normal scheduling, partition, QOS, etc.). If jobs are still running when you RESUME, the node will reflect its current allocation; once those jobs finish it will show idle and can accept new jobs.

What the commands control
- Preventing new allocations: DRAIN stops the scheduler from placing additional jobs on the node(s) immediately.
- Running jobs: DRAIN does not forcibly stop or requeue currently running jobs. They run to completion unless you separately scancel or requeue them.
- Pending jobs: Jobs already allocated to a node (e.g., in CONFIGURING) will still proceed; jobs that would otherwise be scheduled to that node will not be assigned while it is drained.
- RESUME: removes the DRAIN flag/mark and returns the node to normal scheduling eligibility.

Common options and notes
- Reason: you can record a human-readable reason when draining (Reason="maintenance") and that reason is shown by node-status tools.
- Visibility: sinfo / scontrol show will show the node state/flags so admins and users can see the drain reason and that allocations are blocked.
- Difference from DOWN/FAIL: DRAIN is an administrative prevention of new allocations (for maintenance, etc.). DOWN or NODE_FAIL indicate node failure/unavailability — those states are used for nodes that have problems and may have different scheduler/cleanup behavior.
- Forcing behavior: if you want running jobs removed or requeued when taking a node out of service, you must take explicit action (scancel, scontrol requeue/hold, or use other scontrol options); DRAIN alone does not perform that.
- Timing: a node set to DRAIN becomes ineligible for new allocations immediately; its apparent state (allocated vs idle) will continue to reflect current jobs until those jobs end or are removed.

Examples
- Drain with a reason:
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=DRAIN Reason="kernel upgrade"
- Make node usable again:
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=RESUME

Behavior summary
- DRAIN = block new allocations; let current allocations finish.
- RESUME = clear the drain, restore normal eligibility for scheduling.

That covers the intended semantics and typical admin usage for State=DRAIN and State=RESUME.

results.prompt: Explain sdiag scheduler diagnostic fields
results.agent_response:
sdiag reports counters and timing metrics from slurmctld that help diagnose scheduler behavior (threads, RPC/agent activity, job lifecycle, scheduling/backfill work, and cycle timing). Below are the common fields you will see and what each means.

Global / slurmctld execution
- Server thread count — number of active slurmctld threads handling RPCs and internal work; high values indicate heavy slurmctld load.
- RPC/agent counts — counts of agent/RPC activity (connections, created agents, RPC requests). spikes show increased client or controller activity.

Job lifecycle counters
- Jobs submitted / launched / completed / failed / cancelled / requeued / resumed — cumulative counters of job state transitions seen by slurmctld since the last reset. Use these to understand submission/completion rates and error volume.
- Steps created / steps completed — counts for job steps (task-level entities) created and finished.

Scheduling cycle timing and counts
- Scheduling cycle count — number of scheduler iterations (how many times the scheduler loop ran).
- Cycle time (min / avg / max) — how long scheduler iterations are taking; long or widely varying cycle times indicate expensive scheduling work or resource contention inside slurmctld.
- Work items per cycle / evaluated jobs per cycle — how much work the scheduler is doing each iteration.

Backfill and scheduling-plugin statistics
- Backfill evaluations / accepted / rejected (or similar) — how often the backfill logic examines pending jobs and whether they were allowed to run; useful to see whether backfill is effective.
- Backfill window / backfill checks — counts/metrics indicating how many potential placements the backfiller inspected; very large counts indicate heavy backfill computation.

Resource / allocation activity
- Node updates / node state changes — how many node status updates or reconfigurations slurmctld processed.
- Allocation/TRES changes — counters of resource allocation events (CPUs, GPUs, memory) handled.

Other diagnostic counters
- Preemptions / evictions / reservations handled — counts of preemption or reservation actions the scheduler took.
- Deferred/gang/heterogeneous job bookkeeping — counters related to special scheduling behaviors (if used).

Operational notes for interpretation
- sdiag shows cumulative counters reset at midnight UTC by default; use sdiag --reset to zero counters when you want to measure a fresh interval.
- High server thread count, large numbers of RPCs, or long scheduler cycle times indicate controller load; investigate submission rates, polling/monitoring clients, or expensive scheduling rules/plugins.
- Large backfill evaluation counts with few accepts can indicate inaccurate time limits on running jobs or an overly expensive backfill policy.
- Use sdiag sparingly: each invocation is an RPC to slurmctld and frequent calls can affect controller performance.

Output formats / options
- sdiag -a (default) prints the full set of counters; --json is available for machine parsing.
- There is a --reset option to clear the counters after you capture a baseline.

## Backfill Scheduling [#backfill](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.
Backfill scheduling will start lower priority jobs if doing so does not delay
the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.
Since the expected start time of pending jobs depends upon the expected
completion time of running jobs, reasonably accurate time limits are important
for backfill scheduling to work well.

results.prompt: Explain sdiag scheduler diagnostic fields
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise field-by-field explanation of the common sdiag (scheduler diagnostics) output and how to interpret each metric.

General notes
- sdiag --all is the usual mode; sdiag --reset clears the counters (they’re also reset automatically at midnight UTC by default).
- You can emit JSON (--json) for programmatic parsing.
- sdiag reports counters and timing information about slurmctld behavior (threads, RPCs/agents, scheduling cycles, backfill/reservations, job dispatching). High counts or long times generally indicate load or scheduler work that may need tuning.

Primary fields and meaning

- Server thread count
  - Number of active slurmctld threads. A higher number means slurmctld is processing many concurrent tasks (submits, completions, RPCs). Persistently high values can indicate heavy load.

- Agent thread count
  - Number of worker/agent threads used by slurmctld to perform asynchronous work. Similar interpretation to server threads; growth signals concurrent internal work.

- Scheduling cycle count (or Scheduler cycles)
  - How many scheduling iterations the controller has performed. Each cycle examines the queue and attempts to dispatch eligible jobs.

- Avg / Min / Max scheduling cycle time
  - Timing statistics (often in microseconds or milliseconds) for scheduling iterations:
    - Avg cycle time: typical cost of a scheduler iteration.
    - Max cycle time: worst-case iteration — useful to spot occasional expensive computations.
  - Long average or large max times mean the scheduler is spending a lot of CPU/time evaluating the queue (could be many jobs, complex constraints, or expensive backfill evaluation).

- Jobs considered / Jobs examined (per cycle or total)
  - How many pending jobs the scheduler looked at while deciding what to start. High ratio of considered→started indicates wasted work if many are repeatedly re-examined but never run.

- Jobs started / Jobs dispatched
  - Number of jobs the scheduler actually launched. Compare to “jobs considered” to judge efficiency.

- Jobs rejected / Jobs deferred / Jobs failed to start
  - Jobs that could not be scheduled (due to policies, resources, time limits, or heterogeneous constraints) or that failed during allocation. Use these to find scheduling bottlenecks or misconfigurations.

- Backfill statistics (Backfill windows / Backfill attempts / Backfill jobs started / Backfill failures)
  - Counts/timings for the backfill algorithm:
    - How many candidate backfill windows were evaluated.
    - How many backfill-starts succeeded vs. deferred/failed.
  - Large numbers of attempted windows with few starts suggest fragmentation or unsuitable job time limits.

- Reservation checks / Reservation evaluations
  - How often reservations are consulted during scheduling. Useful if you use advance/reservation-based allocations.

- Queue scan totals / Queue scan time
  - Aggregate time spent scanning the job queue (often separate from cycle time). High values point to expensive queue evaluation (many jobs, complex constraints).

- RPC / Event counters
  - Counts of RPCs or events processed by slurmctld (client requests, plugin calls, etc.). High RPC rates may indicate heavy client activity or monitoring tools over-querying slurmctld.

- Priority/fairshare evaluations (if present)
  - Number/timing of priority calculations. Expensive priority computations (many users/accounts) will increase scheduler cycle time.

How to use sdiag data
- Look for correlations: high Avg cycle time + many jobs considered + few jobs started = inefficient scheduling or resource fragmentation.
- Use Max cycle time to find occasional expensive iterations (helps track down specific problematic jobs or constraints).
- If backfill is expensive (many windows tried), encourage users to set realistic time limits or tune backfill parameters.
- If RPC or thread counts are high, investigate frequent client calls (monitoring scripts, polling) or scale scheduler resources.
- Use --json for automation and --reset to get a fresh baseline after making config changes.

If you want, tell me the exact sdiag output you have (paste it) and I’ll point to the specific fields in that output and what to investigate.

## System Administrator Information [#sys_admin](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The job submit plugin is invoked independently for each component of a
heterogeneous job.
The spank_init_post_opt() function is invoked once for each component of a
heterogeneous job. This permits site defined options on a per job component

## Limitations [#limitations](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The backfill scheduler has limitations in how it tracks usage of CPUs and
memory in the future.
This typically requires the backfill scheduler be able to allocate each
component of a heterogeneous job on a different node in order to begin its
resource allocation, even if multiple components of the job do actually get
allocated resources on the same node.
In a federation of clusters, a heterogeneous job will execute entirely on
the cluster from which the job is submitted. The heterogeneous job will not
be eligible to migrate between clusters or to have different components of
the job execute on different clusters in the federation.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sdiag.html)
Executing sdiag sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sdiag to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Explain sbatch mail notification options
results.agent_response:
Summary
- sbatch supports two related options to send email about job events:
  - --mail-user=<user@host> (or #SBATCH --mail-user=...) — destination address(es).
  - --mail-type=<TYPE[,TYPE...]> (or #SBATCH --mail-type=...) — which events trigger mail.

Common usage
- In a batch script:
  #SBATCH --mail-user=alice@example.com
  #SBATCH --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL
- On the command line:
  sbatch --mail-user=alice@example.com --mail-type=END,FAIL myjob.sh

mail-type basics
- Accepts a comma-separated list of event names.
- Typical event names: BEGIN (job started), END (job finished), FAIL (job failed), REQUEUE (job requeued).
- ALL requests all supported notifications; NONE disables notifications.
- Many Slurm releases also provide additional types (for example, time-limit warnings such as TIME_LIMIT or percent warnings like TIME_LIMIT_90, and other events). Check your sbatch man page for the complete set available on your system.

mail-user and defaults
- If you set mail-type but do not set mail-user, mail is sent to the submitting user’s default address.
- You may list multiple addresses (comma-separated) depending on site config.

Precedence / where to set
- You can specify options in the script with #SBATCH directives, via environment variables (SBATCH_*), or on the sbatch command line.
- Command-line options override environment variables; environment variables override #SBATCH lines in a script.

Notes
- The controller sends the messages when the corresponding event occurs; content and formatting are controlled by Slurm and site mail configuration.
- If you need exact mail-type names supported on your cluster, check the sbatch man page (man sbatch) because available types can vary by Slurm version and site configuration.

results.prompt: Explain sbatch mail notification options
results.agent_response:
sbatch provides two options to control e‑mail notifications for a job:

- --mail-user=ADDRESS
  - Set the destination e‑mail address for notifications (example: --mail-user=you@example.com).
  - Can be given on the sbatch command line or as a #SBATCH directive in the job script.

- --mail-type=TYPE[,TYPE...]
  - Select which job events trigger an e‑mail. Multiple events are provided as a comma‑separated list.
  - Common event types you will see documented and can use include: BEGIN, END, FAIL, REQUEUE, ALL, NONE, ARRAY_TASKS, TIME_LIMIT, STAGE_OUT, NODE_FAIL.
    - BEGIN: send when the job allocation starts.
    - END: send when the job finishes normally.
    - FAIL: send when the job fails (non‑zero exit or other failure conditions).
    - REQUEUE: send when the job is requeued.
    - TIME_LIMIT: send when the job reaches (or is about to reach, depending on configuration) its time limit.
    - ARRAY_TASKS: send notifications for individual array tasks rather than only the master array job.
    - ALL: shorthand for getting notifications for all (or most) events.
    - NONE: disable notifications (or omit --mail-type to get no mail).
    - STAGE_OUT / NODE_FAIL: other system/cluster-specific events may be available on some installs.
  - Use e.g. --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL to get mail at start, successful end, and failure.

Examples:
- sbatch --mail-user=you@example.com --mail-type=END myscript.sh
- In a script:
  #SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
  #SBATCH --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL

Notes and caveats:
- The cluster’s mail/send subsystem (sendmail/postfix or similar) must be configured; if the admin has disabled mail or the MTA is misconfigured you may not receive mail.

Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If

in a denial of service.

results.prompt: Explain sbatch mail notification options
results.agent_response:
sbatch supports a small set of mail-related options you use to tell Slurm when to send job-status email and where to send it.

How to set them
- On the sbatch command line:
  - --mail-user=<address>
  - --mail-type=<type>[,<type>...]
- In a batch script use #SBATCH directives:
  - #SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
  - #SBATCH --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL
- Environment variables are also supported (e.g., SBATCH_MAIL_USER, SBATCH_MAIL_TYPE). Note the precedence: command-line options override environment variables, and environment variables override #SBATCH directives in the script.

Common mail-type values and meaning
- NONE — do not send any mail.
- BEGIN — send mail when the job begins (allocation granted / job started).
- END — send mail when the job finishes (regardless of success/failure).
- FAIL — send mail when the job fails (abnormal exit/failed).
- REQUEUE — send mail if the job is requeued.
- ALL — shorthand to request all the common notifications (convenience alias).
- TIME_LIMIT / TIME_LIMIT_xx (percent thresholds) — send warning when job is approaching its time limit (clusters may provide variants like TIME_LIMIT_90 etc.; exact names available in your Slurm docs/config).
- ARRAY_TASKS — affects array-element notifications (send per-array-element notices).

Usage notes and tips
- You can supply multiple types as a comma-separated list (e.g., --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL).
- Use --mail-user to give one or more recipient addresses (site policy may affect allowed formats).
- Email notifications depend on MTA/configuration on your cluster; administrators can disable or alter mail delivery.
- For job arrays, use the array-specific mail-type (or ARRAY_TASKS) to control element-level messages.
- If you need fine-grained control beyond these built-in events, consider writing a small wrapper in your batch script to send mail (mailx, sendmail, curl to an alert webhook) at any programmatic point.

If you want, I can show exact --mail-type tokens supported on your cluster (and any cluster-specific behavior) — ask and I’ll look them up in your Slurm docs/config.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:

## System Administration [#administration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A new configuration parameter has been added to control the maximum
job array size: MaxArraySize . The smallest index that can be specified
by a user is zero and the maximum index is MaxArraySize minus one.
The default value of MaxArraySize is 1001.
The maximum MaxArraySize supported in Slurm is 4000001.
Be mindful about the value of MaxArraySize as job arrays offer an easy way
for users to submit large numbers of jobs very quickly.
The sched/backfill plugin has been modified to improve performance with
job arrays. Once one element of a job array is discovered to not be runnable
or impact the scheduling of pending jobs, the remaining elements of that job
array will be quickly skipped.
Slurm creates a single job record when a job array is submitted.

## Common Reasons [#common_reasons](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_reason_codes.html)
- AssocGrp* — The job's association has reached an aggregate [limit](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html).
- AssocMax* — A portion of the job request exceeds a maximum [limit](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html) (e.g., PerJob, PerNode) for the requested association.
- BeginTime — The job's earliest [start time](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) has not yet been reached.
- Dependency — This job has a [dependency](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) on another job that has not been satisfied.
- Max*PerAccount — A portion of the job request exceeds the per-Account [limit](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html) on the job's [QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
